status: DRAFT — NOT FROZEN. Collection must not begin against this file.
purpose: Candidate item set for the second instrument in prereg/PREREG-2026-09-12-instrument-choice.md. Authored for the author to cut, not to ship as-is.

axes.grounding: higher law <-> will-to-power. Does the actor submit to a law, court, election or plain fact ABOVE its own program, when that authority tells it no?
axes.method: open <-> authoritarian. How does it treat dissent: argue and tolerate, or suppress and compel?
axes.reversibility: reversible <-> ratcheted. Can the gain be argued, voted or litigated back, or does each click hold?

response_grammar: Strongly Disagree | Disagree | Agree | Strongly Agree — identical to the retired questionnaire's arm, so the instrument is the only difference between arms.
loading: +1: agreement moves toward the HEALTHY pole (higher-law / open / reversible). -1: agreement moves toward the unhealthy pole. Half of each axis is reverse-keyed so acquiescence bias cannot masquerade as a position.
favors: Which side the HEALTHY answer lands on: 'establishment' = the answer a currently dominant institution would give; 'dissident' = the answer an opposition would give. The symmetry requirement is that each axis is near-balanced on this field. An instrument whose healthy pole always favours one side is measuring the faction, not the axis.
authoring_notes: Every item describes an ACTION or a situation resolving one way, never a value the respondent holds. 'Dissent should be tolerated' is excluded by the prereg; 'a regulator reissues a struck-down rule under a different statute' is the admissible form.

No item names a living person, a party, or a currently-contested policy by name. The axes are supposed to sort across eras and labels, and a named referent imports the left/right mask the instrument exists to avoid.
One axis per item. Several drafts that loaded two were cut rather than reworded, because a two-axis item is unscoreable against a per-axis claim.

items.text: A government agency loses a court challenge to its flagship programme and suspends the programme while it appeals.
After a court strikes down a rule, the agency reissues substantially the same rule under a different statutory authority.
A protest movement that has won a concession accepts a court ruling that limits how far the concession extends.
An insurgent movement that wins power dismisses the judges who had ruled against it before the election.
An incumbent administration certifies an election result it lost without conditioning certification on a further review.
A body that has been told by an auditor that its figures are wrong redefines the measure so the figures become right.
A campaign publishes the evidence that undercuts its own strongest claim rather than holding it back.
A movement treats a law it disagrees with as void for its own members while demanding the law bind its opponents.
A ministry complies with a freedom-of-information order that will embarrass it, on the deadline set by the tribunal.
An executive declares that an inconvenient constitutional provision does not apply during the period it defines as an emergency.
An advocacy group that obtains leaked documents redacts the material that would endanger uninvolved people before publishing.
A faction argues that because its cause is just, the procedural rules that would slow it are illegitimate.
A regulator that has been overruled publishes the reasoning of the body that overruled it alongside its own.
An institution responds to an adverse finding by replacing the panel that produced it and commissioning a new one.
A dissident organisation submits to an external audit of its own finances on the same terms it demands of the state.
A movement claims a divine or historical mandate that it says places its programme beyond ordinary legal challenge.
An agency abandons a policy after the evidence it cited is shown to be mistaken, without waiting to be compelled.
A department retains a contested practice by moving it to a body that the relevant oversight statute does not cover.
An opposition party that wins on a promise to repeal an emergency power repeals it while still holding office.
A group that gains control of an institution reinterprets its founding charter to remove the limits that had constrained the previous holders.
A public body publishes the submissions that argued against the decision it ultimately took.
An agency asks payment processors to withdraw service from a lawful organisation whose views it opposes.
A campaigning organisation hosts a debate with the researcher whose findings most damage its position.
Activists successfully pressure a venue to cancel a talk rather than protest it while it goes ahead.
A licensing authority renews the licence of a broadcaster that has campaigned against the authority's own remit.
A regulator issues guidance that intermediaries should remove lawful speech it classifies as harmful.
A movement expels a member for threatening a critic rather than defending the threat as passion.
A group publishes the employer and home area of a person whose opinions it opposes so that others may act on it.
An institution that loses an internal vote records the dissenting reasoning in the published minutes.
A body makes continued funding of research groups conditional on their conclusions not contradicting its stated position.
An opposition newspaper prints a correction of its own story at the same prominence as the original.
A faction shouts down a speaker on the grounds that permitting the speech would itself be a harm.
An authority responds to an unauthorised leak by contesting its accuracy in public rather than by prosecuting the publisher.
An agency maintains a list of citizens whose lawful public statements it monitors for institutional risk.
A protest organisation publishes its stewards' rules for handling counter-protesters and holds its members to them.
A movement treats those who disagree on method, rather than on aim, as enemies to be removed from the coalition.
A department declassifies the internal objections to a policy at the same time it announces the policy.
An official body funds a programme to correct public opinion on a question that remains politically contested.
A group that has been censored declines to censor its own opponents when it later controls the platform.
A coalition makes membership conditional on public affirmation of a position unrelated to the coalition's purpose.
An emergency power is written with an expiry date and lapses on that date without renewal.
Powers taken during an emergency remain in force after the emergency is officially declared over.
A movement that wins a change supports a scheduled review at which the change could be undone.
A campaign entrenches its win in a form deliberately designed to be difficult for a later majority to reverse.
A department dismantles the data collection built for a programme once the programme ends.
An identity system introduced for one narrow purpose is extended to further purposes without fresh authorisation.
An organisation that gains an exemption accepts that the exemption expires with the circumstances that justified it.
A group that captures an institution changes the rules for removing its leadership before those rules could be used.
A surveillance capability is retired and its stored material destroyed when the authorising statute lapses.
A temporary measure is renewed at each expiry for long enough that its removal is treated as a radical proposal.
A reform is enacted by ordinary legislation that a later ordinary majority could repeal.
A change is placed in an international instrument specifically so that domestic reversal becomes impracticable.
An authority publishes, in advance, the conditions under which a new power would be withdrawn.
Infrastructure built for a reversible policy is designed so that removing the policy would not remove the capability.
A movement that obtains an emergency exception opposes its extension once the emergency passes.
A faction makes a procedural change to win a present dispute and then opposes reverting it when the dispute ends.
A registry created for a programme is closed and its records deleted when the programme is discontinued.
A discretionary power granted for an exceptional case becomes the routine route for ordinary cases.
An organisation that wins control of a standard-setting body leaves the appeal route that its predecessors used against it intact.
A group secures its gain by making the body that could reverse it dependent on the group for funding.
